column5: hands held steady until sunset
column6: The commentary distinguishes a person holding himself from another holding his hand, then extends patience to a group; Aaron and Hur physically support Moses' tired hands until sunset while the people endure battle.

column5: remember prisoners as bound with them
column6: The commentary's person held by others remains part of the patient community; Hebrews tells readers to remember prisoners as though bound alongside them, turning shared endurance into solidarity.

column5: visit the one held in prison
column6: The commentary places the captive beside the hand that may withhold good; the righteous are commended for coming to the speaker while he was in prison, an action addressed specifically to the held person.

column5: failure to visit prisoner
column6: The commentary's withholding hand and detained person meet in one moral scene; the condemned are told they did not visit the speaker when he was sick or in prison.

column5: wrongdoer held by cords of his sin
column6: The commentary says each person is held to what he has earned; the proverb makes that relation physical when the wicked person's own iniquities ensnare him and the cords of his sin hold him fast.

column5: holy ones handed over for a limited time
column6: The commentary speaks of an afflicted group that must endure together; Daniel's arrogant king wears out the holy ones and they are given into his hand for a stated time before the kingdom changes hands.

column5: gain life through endurance
column6: The commentary calls humanity lost except for those who practice patience; Jesus tells persecuted hearers that by their endurance they will gain their lives, linking loss and preservation directly.

column5: discipline body and make it a slave
column6: The commentary sets holding oneself beside being held by another; Paul says he disciplines and enslaves his own body lest he be disqualified, deliberately combining the two positions in one person.

column5: strengthen weak hands
column6: The commentary moves from a person's restraining hand to mutual encouragement; Isaiah commands hearers to strengthen weak hands, making the community's support of frail members concrete.

column5: say to the anxious to be strong
column6: The commentary's believers recommend patience to one another under divine care; Isaiah tells them to address fearful hearts with courage and the promise that God will come and save.

column5: speak truth to one another
column6: The commentary's exception to loss includes mutual counsel in truth; Zechariah commands people to speak truth with their neighbors and render true judgments for peace, giving that counsel a public setting.

column5: truth spoken because members belong together
column6: The commentary joins truth to reciprocal counsel within the group; Ephesians tells each person to speak truth to a neighbor because believers are members of one another.

column5: teach and admonish one another
column6: The commentary says the saved community commends truth and patience to its members; Colossians commands mutual teaching and admonition with wisdom, turning shared conviction into speech.

column5: reprove neighbor instead of harboring wrong
column6: The commentary's mutual counsel requires another person's good; the law commands frank correction of a neighbor rather than silently bearing sin on his account.

column5: oath threatens an unwitting eater with death
column6: The commentary's forced oath and captive held for killing are separate senses of restraint; Saul's oath leads him to pronounce death on Jonathan for eating honey, showing how an imposed restraint can endanger a person.

column5: community rescues person condemned by oath
column6: The commentary makes endurance and right action communal; Saul's people refuse to let Jonathan die under the oath and rescue him, countering imposed restraint through collective intervention.

column5: Shimei ordered to remain in one city
column6: The commentary's passive patient is held by another's command; Solomon orders Shimei to build a house in Jerusalem and stay there, making domestic residence a form of custody.

column5: king recalls oath tied to confinement
column6: The commentary names a man compelled to swear and then held under another's control; Solomon reminds Shimei of the oath attached to his Jerusalem confinement after he crossed its boundary.

column5: confinement and oath end in execution
column6: The commentary's coerced oath can converge with being held for death; Solomon orders Shimei executed after finding he violated the oath governing his residence.

column5: oath-bound abstinence used to plan murder
column6: The commentary calls fasting a type of self-restraint yet also depicts forced oath and a person held for death; conspirators bind themselves by an oath to eat and drink nothing until they kill Paul, turning restraint into violence.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound match; shut rain
column6: The commentary's asr includes holding back, and its grain is protected from loss; God warns that he may shut the heavens so rain and produce cease, using the table's Hebrew עצר correspondence for a communal loss of harvest.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's held grain and waiting community depend on what is released; Solomon envisions heaven restrained from rain because of sin and asks that prayer and repentance be heard, using עצר for divine withholding.

column5: wait for the delayed appointed time
column6: The commentary presents patience as waiting for the Lord's decision; Habakkuk says the vision has an appointed time and instructs the hearer to wait even if it delays.

column5: faithfulness amid the delayed vision
column6: The commentary joins belief to patience as the exception to loss; Habakkuk contrasts the proud person's disordered soul with the righteous one who lives by faithfulness in the delay described just before.

column5: one who trusts need not hurry
column6: The commentary sets belief and patient restraint against the human being's haste; Isaiah says the person who trusts the tested foundation will not be hurried, joining trust to freedom from panic.

column5: quiet trust offered but refused
column6: The commentary says salvation belongs to those who restrain themselves in faith; God tells Judah that quietness and trust would be their strength, then says they were unwilling, making refusal of patience explicit.

column5: flight chosen instead of stillness
column6: The commentary's hasty human will not hold himself; Judah chooses swift horses rather than quiet trust and is told that flight and pursuit will follow, a concrete outcome of the refusal in the previous verse.

column5: slow speech and slow anger
column6: The commentary opposes the human being's quick distress to holding the self; James commands everyone to be quick to hear but slow to speak and slow to anger.

column5: slow anger versus hasty folly
column6: The commentary's patience is the contrary of impulsive human outcry; the proverb contrasts a person slow to anger with one quick tempered who exalts folly.

column5: do not hasten to anger in spirit
column6: The commentary makes patience the restraining of inner agitation; Ecclesiastes warns against being quick in spirit to anger because anger lodges with fools.

column5: stored goods mistaken for long rest
column6: The commentary opposes prudent waiting to a hand that hoards; the rich farmer tells his soul to rest for many years on stored goods, an imagined secure future overturned by the divine demand in the next verse.

column5: Satan seeks to sift disciples like wheat
column6: The commentary's grain is kept in its covering and the community must endure pressure; Jesus says Satan has demanded to sift the disciples like wheat, turning grain processing into an image of testing the group.

column5: prayer protects faith through sifting
column6: The commentary's waiting believer is under protective divine attention and encourages others; Jesus says he has prayed that Peter's faith not fail and tells him to strengthen his brothers after he turns back.

column5: naked grain sown without its mature covering
column6: The commentary pictures grain guarded by a surrounding husk; Paul says what is sown is a bare grain rather than the body it will have, placing fruitfulness at the point where the old covering is relinquished.

column5: self-control and prayer near the end
column6: The commentary links the passing time, the held self and an exception marked by prayer; Peter says the end is near and therefore calls believers to sound judgment and sobriety for prayer.

column5: firm faith amid shared suffering
column6: The commentary extends patience from one person to a mutually enduring community; Peter tells believers to resist firmly in faith, knowing the same sufferings are being completed among their brothers and sisters elsewhere.

column5: care for prisoners despite property loss
column6: The commentary sets imprisoned people beside the hand that guards possessions; Hebrews recalls sympathy for prisoners and joyful acceptance of property being seized because the community knew of a better possession.

column5: God's patience delays destruction
column6: The commentary says waiting occurs under God's watch and ends in judgment; this verse interprets apparent divine delay as patience toward people, giving them time to repent rather than perish.

column5: conduct measured against coming fire
column6: The commentary ties daring toward fire to a ruinous moral choice; after describing the world's fiery dissolution, Peter asks what holy and godly conduct is required, reversing reckless exposure into ethical preparation.

column5: divine forbearance meant for repentance
column6: The commentary treats patience as a held response to wrongdoing; Paul says God's kindness, forbearance and patience are meant to lead the human being to repentance, extending restraint to God.

column5: storing wrath through stubbornness
column6: The commentary's person can hoard what becomes loss at judgment; Paul says a hard, unrepentant heart stores up wrath for the day of God's judgment, a negative counterpart to storing goods.

column5: divine patience toward those facing destruction
column6: The commentary sets patient restraint beside judgment on the human being; Paul describes God enduring with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, delaying the punitive end.

column5: ء ن س / אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB Arabic note
column6: The commentary's insan is in loss except for right action; Eliphaz asks whether mortal enosh can be righteous before God, pressing the frail human term into a question about moral standing.

column5: ء ن س / אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB Arabic note
column6: The commentary's insan stands inside passing time; the psalm compares the days of mortal enosh to grass and a field flower, making human duration visibly fragile.

column5: unjust gain used to build a safe nest
column6: The commentary's withholding hand tries to protect what it has gathered; Habakkuk condemns one who gains evil profit for his house to place his nest high beyond disaster.

column5: hoarder's plan costs his own life
column6: The commentary's possessor becomes the one in loss; Habakkuk says the plan to cut off many peoples has brought shame on the house and forfeited its maker's life, undoing the security sought in the prior verse.

column5: mouth put in dust while hope remains
column6: The commentary describes patience as holding back the cry while awaiting deliverance; after the instruction to sit silently under a yoke, Lamentations bids the sufferer put his mouth in dust because hope may remain.

column5: prisoner asks release and righteous company
column6: The commentary's held person needs both rescue and the community's patient support; in Hebrew verse numbering the psalmist asks to be brought out of confinement so he can praise God among the righteous.

column5: friend strengthens threatened man's hand
column6: The commentary moves from a restraining hand to mutually commended endurance; Jonathan comes to David in danger and strengthens his hand in God, turning the hand into an image of encouragement.

column5: prisoners told to come out
column6: The commentary's passive patient is held by another; the servant's commission includes telling prisoners to come out and those in darkness to show themselves, reversing enforced enclosure.

column5: kept word of endurance, then guarded from trial
column6: The commentary links mutual persistence with being kept under divine eyes; the risen speaker promises to keep a faithful community from the hour of trial because it has kept his word of endurance.

column5: patient waiting for unseen hope
column6: The commentary's patience means waiting for a divine outcome one cannot yet see; Paul says believers wait for what they do not see through endurance.

column5: faith tested into endurance
column6: The commentary puts faith and patience together as the exception to human loss; James says the testing of faith produces steadfastness, explaining how the two qualities meet in affliction.

column5: endurance prevents lack
column6: The commentary describes humanity as in loss unless patience joins faith and good action; James asks that steadfastness complete its work so the believer may be complete and lack nothing.

column5: endured the cross for a future joy
column6: The commentary contrasts a captive facing death with voluntary patience; Jesus endures the cross and shame for the joy set before him, giving purpose to restraint under execution.

column5: athlete exercises self-control for a crown
column6: The commentary calls fasting a bodily form of holding oneself; Paul says athletes exercise self-control in all things for a perishable crown, then points to an imperishable aim.

column5: long fast brings real hunger
column6: The commentary identifies fasting as one kind of patience; Jesus fasts forty days and nights and becomes hungry, presenting abstinence as bodily restraint with a cost.

column5: hunger teaches dependence beyond bread
column6: The commentary places being restrained beside patient trust; Moses says God humbled Israel by hunger and fed it manna so it would learn to live by what comes from God's mouth, a communal education through withheld food.

column5: fasting savings given to needy people
column6: The commentary places fasting beside the hand that can withhold goods; Hermas' instruction directs a faster to give the cost of the uneaten meal to someone in need, making bodily restraint release resources.

column5: reward of fasting is charity
column6: The commentary pairs fasting as self-restraint with the ethical problem of withholding; this rabbinic maxim makes charity the reward or fruit of a fast, interpreting abstinence through what the hand gives.

column5: give from possessions without turning away
column6: The commentary's withholding hand closes before the needy; Tobit instructs his son to give alms from his possessions and not turn his face from the poor, joining family counsel to generosity.

column5: alms deliver from death
column6: The commentary moves from hoarded goods to a person held toward death; Tobit says almsgiving delivers from death and keeps one from darkness, assigning the opened hand a rescuing effect.

column5: withheld help makes needy eyes wait
column6: The commentary places waiting beside a hand that withholds; Sirach forbids depriving the poor of life and making the needy person's eyes wait, showing how one person's grasping imposes another's patience.

column5: restrain appetites
column6: The commentary defines patience as holding one's own self; Sirach tells the hearer not to follow desires but to restrain appetites, directing the holding inward.

column5: patient acceptance of humiliating change
column6: The commentary asks the afflicted person to wait under God's judgment rather than cry out; Sirach tells the hearer to accept what befalls him and be patient in humiliation.

column5: torturers test a righteous person's forbearance
column6: The commentary's captive held for killing and the patient person can be the same individual; the wicked propose tormenting the righteous man to test his gentleness and forbearance.

column5: righteous person condemned to shameful death
column6: The commentary's passive patient is restrained toward death; the wicked resolve to condemn the tested righteous man to a shameful death while claiming God will protect him, making the test lethal.

column5: devout reason rules passions
column6: The commentary treats patience as holding the self even under pressure; the work opens by arguing that pious reason governs passions, a Jewish interpretation of disciplined endurance developed in its martyr stories.

column5: menstruation imposes contact limits
column6: The commentary's newly menstruating girl is held inside a house; the law assigns seven days of menstrual impurity and limits contact, supplying a ritual background for seclusion without itself ordering house confinement.

column5: father's vow constrains daughter's future
column6: The commentary places a girl under a father's control and also describes forced oath; Jephthah tells his daughter he has vowed to the Lord and cannot take it back, so his own oath determines her fate, though she did not swear it.

column5: part of sale proceeds held back secretly
column6: The commentary's holding hand can turn into deception; Ananias keeps part of the proceeds while presenting a gift as though complete, so the retained amount is tied to false speech.

column5: property remained at the giver's disposal
column6: The commentary's tight hand is blameworthy when it refuses a rightful good; Peter says the field and its price remained under Ananias's authority, specifying that his wrongdoing was deceit rather than mere retention.

column5: harmful designs and false oaths rejected
column6: The commentary's communal truth-telling stands beside a coerced oath; Zechariah forbids plotting evil against a neighbor and loving a false oath, guarding the group against speech used to injure.

column5: mutually encourage and build up
column6: The commentary makes patience something believers counsel each other to practice; Paul directly tells the community to encourage one another and build each other up.

column5: plain yes and no rather than sworn control
column6: The commentary's man is made to swear by someone else; Jesus directs hearers toward plain yes and no, supplying a form of truthful speech that does not depend on an imposed oath.

column5: imprisonment and hunger together
column6: The commentary juxtaposes enforced custody with endurance; Paul lists imprisonments alongside hard work, sleeplessness and hunger among apostolic hardships, preceding the patience named in the next verse.

column5: patience and kindness in hardship
column6: The commentary's patient community has to answer distress with good action; Paul follows the preceding list of prisons and deprivations by naming patience and kindness among the qualities of his ministry.

column5: fasting answered with God's word
column6: The commentary's fast is a kind of self-restraint oriented toward divine judgment; when hungry after fasting, Jesus answers temptation by saying human life depends on God's word as well as bread.

column5: gradual gathering versus hasty wealth
column6: The commentary sets patient holding beside grasping gain; the proverb says wealth gained hastily shrinks while one who gathers little by little increases it, assigning different outcomes to two tempos of acquisition.

column5: feasting rich man before reversal
column6: The commentary links the human hand's surplus to later loss; the rich man dresses luxuriously and feasts every day while Lazarus lies at his gate in the next verse, establishing what could have been shared.
